About this citation

Chapter names are romanised inconsistently in English editions and in this corpus; the archive normalises them here and gives the character form so the identification is unambiguous.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Mencius said: Those who love others are constantly loved by others; those who respect others are constantly respected by others.”
Classical Chinese
“愛人者人恆愛之，敬人者人恆敬之。”

Eight characters in two parallel clauses. The archive's English opens with “Mencius said,” which is the dialogue frame from Lilou II, not part of the maxim itself; searchers looking for the reciprocity line usually drop that frame.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Those who love others are constantly loved by others; those who respect others are constantly respected by others.”
  • “He who loves others is constantly loved by them; he who respects others is constantly respected by them.”

Attribution notes

Mencius, Lilou II (離婁下). The reciprocity formula is Mencius' own; the archive's English includes the narrator's “Mencius said,” which belongs to the dialogue heading rather than to the saying. Quoting the framed version as a freestanding maxim makes the page title start with the author's name twice and hides the content a searcher is matching against.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Mencius

Mencius (Meng Ke, c. 371–c.

Interpretation

Mencius is defending his claim that human nature tends toward goodness, and this is his argument from reciprocity rather than from sentiment. The structure is conditional: love and respect reliably return, so the failure of that return is evidence of something gone wrong rather than of human nature. In Mencius's usage the terms carry obligation, not only feeling — to respect others is to acknowledge their standing. He is making the cultivated person's behaviour the test of the theory.

Why it matters

It reframes a common complaint. Where return does not come, Mencius would have you ask what failed in the practice rather than conclude that people are ungrateful.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Mencius said: Those who love others are constantly…”?

“Mencius said: Those who love others are constantly…” comes from Mencius, Lilou II (離婁下) (c. 4th–3rd century BCE), attributed to Mencius.

What does Mencius mean by love?

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, dignity.

Is the wording of this Mencius quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Mencius said: Those who love others are constantly loved by others; those who respect others are constantly respected by others.” Forms in circulation that differ: Those who love others are constantly loved by others; those who respect others are constantly respected by others. / He who loves others is constantly loved by them; he who respects others is constantly respected by them. The Classical Chinese reads “愛人者人恆愛之，敬人者人恆敬之。”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Mencius, Lilou II (離婁下). The reciprocity formula is Mencius' own; the archive's English includes the narrator's “Mencius said,” which belongs to the dialogue heading rather than to the saying.
